group.passage:
Sergey Belyavskiy had had his mind set on the Dublin International Piano Competition until, in mid-March 2022, he was informed that he had been banned from the competition, along with eight other contestants. The nine of them had one thing in common: nationality. Since the Russian invasion of Ukraine, Russian musicians have been subjected to scrutiny bordering on discrimination in terms of their stance in this military conflict.
Maxim Vengerov, currently the highest-paid violinist, had his Instagram account flooded with inquiries demanding his anti-war statement, following his fellow Russian pianist Evgeny Kissin voicing his opposition to Russia’s aggression. “Your silence is shameful,” read a relatively milder comment. Valery Gergiev, a prominent conductor, was sacked by both orchestras where he served as principal conductor and dropped from coming concerts for not responding to the ultimatum asking him to denounce Russia’s action. In performance after performance, pieces by Russian composers such as Tchaikovsky and Shostakovich are being pulled from the program, cited as “inappropriate at this moment.”
True, a clear message of solidarity should be sent to all caught in this conflict, but does it include a blanket boycott of Russian culture and artists? In the case of the contestants, they were unwillingly brought into this devastating conflict, yet they were punished for being born Russian. Meanwhile, how is excluding from concerts pieces by Tchaikovsky and Shostakovich, both of whom were oppressed by the Russian regime in their days, contributing to the anti-aggression cause? Surely it is understandable that people are upset at what Russia is doing, and hence orchestras or contest hosts believe the immediate severance of ties with whoever has yet to take a side is the best way to pronounce their firm stance. While it may not seem fair that cultural figures are being asked to speak out against the Russian regime, Gergiev’s case demonstrates the worst action to take in this anti-Russian campaign is inaction.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best summary of this passage?

options.A: Classical musicians protesting against Russia’s war on Ukraine.
options.B: How Russian musicians are affected by Russia’s military action.
options.C: Musicians losing their fans and supporters after the war began.
options.D: The impact of war on Russian classical music development.

questions.stem: What is implied about the comment, “Your silence is shameful,” left on Maxim Vengerov’s Instagram account?

options.A: Vengerov was ashamed of what Russia did.
options.B: He often spoke out against Russia.
options.C: Maxim Vengerov didn’t make it clear that he denounced Russia’s action.
options.D: He objected to the stance of his fellow Russian Kissin.

questions.stem: Which of the following is most likely a statement by the host of the Dublin International Piano Contest?

options.A: “Criticism of Russia’s behavior should not lead to the punishment of innocent people who then have to pay for it.”
options.B: “In light of Russia’s actions, we will be unable to include competitors from Russia in the 2022 competition.”
options.C: “It is important to have a position, but it can’t be demanded. We think it’s a matter of individual choice.”
options.D: “Every day brings new escalations, big and small, and no one knows what this will lead to.”

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following is true?

options.A: Gergiev should not have sided with Ukrainians.
options.B: Evgeny Kissin was slow to make clear his stance.
options.C: Tchaikovsky was a composer known for his love for his country.
options.D: The author does not approve of the Dublin Competition’s decision.

tags.topic: boycott of Russian musicians after the invasion of Ukraine
